case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

case_info.explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.
